title: Small words: dA, bile, ki, ya
intro: Spoken Turkish leans on a handful of short, unstressed words that change the tone of a sentence more than its content: *Gel de gör!* (Come and see!), *Çocuk bile biliyor* (Even a child knows), *O kadar yorgundum ki…* (I was so tired that…), *Biliyorsun ya* (You know). This unit takes them one by one: *dA*, *bile*, the conjunction *ki*, *ya*, and six particles of mood: *hani*, *işte*, *acaba*, *sakın*, *bari*, *hele*. None of them has a suffix form, and all are written apart.

sections.title: Gel de gör: dA beyond too

blocks.text: You know *dA* as **too, also** (*Ben de*, [A1 unit 4](gp-de-also)) and in **even if** (*yağsa da*, [B2 unit 1](gp-even-if)). It is always written apart, follows two-way harmony (*de* after front vowels, *da* after back ones) and never turns into *te* or *ta*. Between two clauses, after an imperative or before a negative, it does more.

head: Use
Example
Meaning
rows: I was tired, so I went to bed early.
I called, but he didn't answer.
He came, and early at that!

blocks.text: **After a verb.** Put after the first of two clauses, *dA* links them like **and so** or **and yet**; the meaning comes from the context: *Hastaydım da gelemedim* (I was ill, that's why I couldn't come), *Çok çalıştım da geçemedim* (I studied hard, and still I didn't pass).
**With an imperative.** *Gel de gör* (Come and see), *Otur da bir çay iç* (Sit down and have a tea): a friendly push, often with the optative after it: *Söyle de bilelim* (Tell us, so we know).

**Softening a negative.** Before *değil* or a negative verb, *da* takes the edge off: *O kadar da kötü değil* (It's not that bad), *Pek de pahalı değil* (It's not all that expensive). **Hem de** adds a stronger point to what was just said: *Geldi, hem de erkenden!* *Hem de nasıl!* is **and how!**

items.en: I was ill, that's why I couldn't come.
I studied hard, and still I didn't pass.
Sit down and have a tea.

items.tr: O kadar da zor değil, sen de yapabilirsin.
items.en: It's not that hard, you can do it too.

items.tr: Maçı kazandık, hem de son dakikada!
items.en: We won the match, and in the last minute at that!

blocks.text: The particle never assimilates and never joins the word: *kitap da* (the book too), *Ahmet de*, *gel de*. Written together, *kitapta* and *Ahmet'te* are locatives.

sections.title: Çocuk bile biliyor: even, and already

blocks.text: *Bile* means **even**. It comes right after the word it focuses on: *Çocuk bile biliyor* (Even a child knows), *Annem bile güldü* (Even my mother laughed). With a negative it is **not even**: *Teşekkür bile etmedi* (He didn't even say thank you), *Bir kez bile aramadı* (He didn't call even once).

**Already.** After a verb in the past, *bile* shows surprise at how soon something happened: *Geldi bile!* (He's here already!), *Yemek soğudu bile* (The food has already gone cold), *Maç başladı bile* (The match has already started).

**bile, dA and hatta.** In **even if**, *bile* and *dA* compete, *bile* being stronger: *yağsa da*, *yağsa bile* ([B2 unit 1](gp-even-if)). *Hatta* (in fact, even) opens a clause and often brings *bile* with it: *Türkçeyi çok iyi konuşuyor, hatta şiir bile yazıyor* (He speaks Turkish very well; he even writes poems).

items.en: Even a child knows the answer to this question.
He didn't even say thank you.
He didn't call even once.
The match has already started!
Everyone came, even Murat.

blocks.text: *Bile* follows the word it stresses, never precedes it: *Ali bile biliyor*, not *Bile Ali biliyor*. And *Ali de biliyor* is just **Ali knows too**: *de* adds, *bile* surprises.

sections.title: Öyle yorgunum ki: the conjunction ki

blocks.text: The conjunction *ki*, borrowed from Persian, links a main clause to the clause that follows it: the opposite order from the noun clauses of [B2 unit 4](gp-dik-clauses). You met it in *dedi ki* ([B1 unit 12](gp-direct-speech)). It is written apart and never changes with harmony.

head: Use
Example
Meaning
rows: O kadar yorgundum ki hemen uyudum.
I was so tired that I fell asleep at once.
Öyle güzel bir gol attı ki herkes ayağa kalktı.
He scored such a beautiful goal that everyone stood up.
I know for sure he won't come.
I looked, and the door was open.
Yüksek sesle söyle ki herkes duysun.
Say it out loud so that everyone hears.

blocks.text: **So … that.** *O kadar* or *öyle* comes before the adjective or verb, and *ki* opens the result: *Maç öyle heyecanlıydı ki kimse yerinden kalkmadı* (The match was so exciting that nobody left their seat). This is the most common use of *ki*, and noun clauses have no way of saying it.

**ki or a noun clause?** *Geleceğini biliyorum* and *Biliyorum ki gelecek* both mean **I know he'll come**. The noun clause is the neutral, usual way; with *ki* the first verb gets the weight, and the sentence sounds more spoken or more insistent. After *bak-* or *gör-*, *ki* tells what you found: *Bir de baktım ki herkes gitmiş* (And then I saw that everyone had left).
**At the end of a sentence**, *ki* adds a shrug or a complaint: *Ne yapayım ki?* (What can I do?), *Bilmiyorum ki!* (But I don't know!).

**Apart or attached?** The conjunction *ki* is written apart: *dedi ki*, *öyle güzel ki*. The suffix `-ki` of [A2 unit 10](gp-ki-adjective) is attached: *evdeki*, *bugünkü*, *benimki*. A few words have *ki* fused into them for good: *belki*, *çünkü*, *sanki*, *hâlbuki*, *oysaki* and *mademki* (since, seeing that).

items.tr: O kadar yorgundum ki hemen uyudum.
items.en: I was so tired that I fell asleep at once.

items.tr: Maç öyle heyecanlıydı ki kimse yerinden kalkmadı.
items.en: The match was so exciting that nobody left their seat.

items.tr: Bir de baktım ki herkes gitmiş.
items.en: And then I saw that everyone had left.
Since we've got tickets, let's go to the match.
What can I do?

blocks.text: Never glue the conjunction to the verb: *dedi ki*, *biliyorum ki*, not *dediki*. If you can put a pause before it and a whole clause after it, it is the conjunction.
*Ya* has several jobs, all of them spoken. Some you know: *Ya sen?* (And you?) from A1 and *Ya gelmezse?* (What if he doesn't come?) from [B1 unit 9](b1-u09).

head: Use
Example
Meaning
rows: Ali'yi tanıyorsun ya, o da geliyor.
You know Ali, right? He's coming too.
Ya bu akşam ya yarın gelirim.
I'll come either tonight or tomorrow.

blocks.text: **After a statement**, *ya* reminds the listener of something they already know, or insists on it: *Biliyorsun ya* (You know), *Söylemiştim ya* (I'd told you, hadn't I?). A rising voice makes it a gentle reminder; a falling one, an impatient **I told you**.

**Ya … ya** offers two choices, one of which will happen: *Ya kabul et ya git* (Either accept or leave). The second *ya* is often *ya da*: *Ya otobüsle ya da metroyla gideriz* (We'll go either by bus or by metro). On its own, *ya da* is simply **or** ([A1 unit 12](gp-conjunctions-basic)).

items.tr: Ali'yi tanıyorsun ya, o da maça geliyor.
items.en: You know Ali, right? He's coming to the match too.
I told you, didn't I!
Will they win? Of course!

items.tr: Ya otobüsle ya da metroyla gideriz.
items.en: We'll go either by bus or by metro.

items.tr: Ya bu akşam ya yarın maçı izleriz.
items.en: We'll watch the match either tonight or tomorrow.

blocks.text: In casual speech *ya* is also an exclamation and a filler (*Ya, bırak şimdi!*: Oh, forget it!), which [B2 unit 9](gp-fillers) comes back to.

sections.title: Hani, işte, acaba, sakın, bari, hele

blocks.text: Six more small words set the mood of a sentence: reproach, pointing, wondering, warning, settling for less, urging. Each is easier to learn from its typical sentences than from a definition.

head: Word
What it does
Example
rows: where is…? (a broken promise); you know, remember
*Hani bana bilet alacaktın?* (Weren't you going to buy me a ticket?)
*Acaba bilet kalmış mı?* (I wonder if there are any tickets left.)
don't you dare, be sure not to
at least (when the better thing isn't possible)
*Gelemiyorsan bari ara.* (If you can't come, at least call.)

blocks.text: **Hani** asks where something promised has gone: *Hani bana yardım edecektin?* (Weren't you going to help me?). With *ya* at the end of the clause, it points to something the listener knows: *Hani köşedeki kafe var ya, orada buluşalım* (You know the café on the corner? Let's meet there).

**İşte** points: *İşte otobüs!* (There's the bus!). It also sums up or stresses: *İşte bu yüzden…* (That's exactly why…), *İşte böyle* (That's how it is), *İşte futbol böyle bir şey* (That's football for you).
**Acaba** (I wonder) goes with a question and makes it a thought aloud: *Acaba gelecek mi?* It also softens a request: *Acaba pencereyi açabilir miyim?* (Could I possibly open the window?).
**Sakın** comes before a negative imperative and makes it a warning: *Sakın kimseye söyleme!* (Don't you dare tell anyone!). *Sakın ha!* on its own is **Don't you dare!**
**Bari** settles for the next best thing, with an imperative or an optative: *Bari bir çay iç* (At least have a tea), *Kazanamıyorsak bari berabere kalalım* (If we can't win, let's at least draw).

**Hele** means **especially** after a list (*Herkes sevindi, hele babam!*), and **just** with an imperative, kindly or as a threat: *Hele bir otur* (Just sit down first), *Hele bir geç kal, görürsün!* (Just you be late and you'll see!).

items.en: Weren't you going to buy me a ticket?
That's exactly why I love you.
I wonder if the match has started.
Don't you dare tell anyone!
If you can't come, at least call.
Everyone was really happy, especially my dad!

blocks.text: Several have French partners: *işte* is often **voilà**, *bari* **au moins**, *acaba* **je me demande si**, and *hani* in a reproach is like **alors, et le billet que tu devais m'acheter ?**

summary: *dA* is written apart and never becomes *te* or *ta*. Beyond **too** it means **and so**, **and yet** (*Aradım da açmadı*), **and** after an imperative (*Gel de gör*), and softens a negative (*O kadar da zor değil*).
*Bile* follows the word it stresses: **even** (*Çocuk bile biliyor*), **not even** with a negative (*Teşekkür bile etmedi*), **already** after a past verb (*Geldi bile!*).

The conjunction *ki* opens the second clause: *O kadar yorgundum ki…*, *Baktım ki…*, *Biliyorum ki…*. Written apart; the suffix `-ki` is attached; *belki, çünkü, sanki, hâlbuki, oysaki, mademki* are one word.
*Ya* reminds (*Biliyorsun ya*), insists (*Söyledim ya!*), asks **what about** (*Ya sen?*) and **what if** (*Ya gelmezse?*), and gives two choices with *ya … ya (da)*.

*Hani* reproaches or reminds, *işte* points and sums up, *acaba* wonders, *sakın* warns before a negative imperative, *bari* settles for **at least**, *hele* stresses **especially** or urges **just**.
